rationale:
This slate follows this week's growth playbook. Every piece stays inside the GLP-1 focus, with tirzepatide first wherever the evidence allows.

**Long-form (L1): "What Happens When You Stop Tirzepatide?"**
- **Why this topic:** it's next in the playbook's Lane A order and the strongest topic on the radar (momentum 86). Lane A videos earn about 8× the watch minutes of our other long-forms.
- **Why not hair loss:** the hair-loss long-form already shipped on 11-02. Fixing it is a QA re-render by the publisher, not a new slot.
- **Why this isn't a repeat:** L1 10-27 on this topic never published (its narration lost numbers), so viewers haven't seen it. The 09-29 long-form was a different angle: an observational study of veterans with type 2 diabetes.
- **Why it can pass fact-check:** the body rests on settled, randomized evidence. That's SURMOUNT-4, with the locked figures from the craft notes (783 began the lead-in, then 335 vs 335 were randomized, and the placebo group regained 14.0% from week 36 to week 88). Mechanism comes from label and mechanism sources.
- **What it must include:** the "don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own" line, and no mention of cost.
- **What it does for the cluster:** it answers a question no live Lane A video answers. The publisher can link it to How Long and Plateau, which helps the stalled How Long.

**Shorts**
- **S1, 08:00, body-worry reassurance:**
  - **Topic:** "Will tirzepatide weaken my bones?" It's an emerging hook (Medscape, 2 Nov), and our earlier bones Short reached 242 views.
  - **Evidence:** handled honestly and observationally. Most studies show no fracture link for GLP-1 medicines, but one cohort flagged tirzepatide (HR 1.44).
  - **Rules it follows:** no hair Short this week, as the playbook asks.
  - **Next step:** it points viewers to the live Bones & Muscle video.
- **S2, 13:00, lead:** retatrutide "what's confirmed?"
  - **Format:** a loop ending, the format that drew 207–274 views before.
  - **Hook:** a fresh liver-injury case report (3 Nov) and the Victoria alert.
  - **Rules it follows:** it uses the week's single gray-market Short. It includes the line that retatrutide isn't approved and that "research" products aren't the trial drug.
- **S3, 20:00, funnel (Exp D) and spin-off of L1:**
  - **Question:** does tirzepatide keep working after month 9?
  - **New fact:** the continued-tirzepatide arm of SURMOUNT-4. The 10-27 Short used the placebo regain figure, so this hasn't been covered.
  - **Next step:** it sends viewers to L1, with Plateau as a nearby video.

**Carousel (C1)**
- **What it is:** a minimum-effort reuse of the verified 11-02 injection-site Short text, because carousels reach almost no one.

**Mix**
- **Trend stages:** 2 emerging or rising (S1, S2), 2 evergreen (L1, C1) and 1 myth-correction (S3).
- **Body systems:** bones, weight maintenance, liver safety and skin, so no organ appears three times.
- **Pillars:** none used more than twice.

pieces.topic: What happens when you stop tirzepatide: the SURMOUNT-4 randomized withdrawal trial (adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes), why appetite signals return, and evidence-based habits that support results
pieces.angle: Opening line, use exactly: 'If you stop tirzepatide, some of the weight you lost tends to come back. In the main trial, people switched to placebo regained part of it on average, while people who stayed on tirzepatide kept losing a little more on average.' Ch2: 'Placebo group: average regain of 14.0% from week 36 to week 88. Tirzepatide group: a further average loss of 5.5% over the same weeks. These are group averages, not predictions for any one person.' Say 'adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes' at least once. Keep 'Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own.', 'Not personal advice' and the full prescriber line.
pieces.working_title: What Happens When You Stop Tirzepatide?
pieces.target_keyword: what happens when you stop tirzepatide
pieces.why: It's next in the playbook's Lane A order and the top radar topic (momentum 86). The 10-27 version never shipped, it rests on settled randomized evidence, and no live Lane A video answers it. | fact-check: Good Lane A topic, well in scope. SURMOUNT-4 (Aronne et al., JAMA 2024) checks out: 783 started the open-label lead-in, then 670 were randomized at week 36 (335 vs 335). The placebo group regained an average of 14.0% from week 36 to week 88, and the group that stayed on tirzepatide lost a further 5.5% on average. Copy the exact figure and wording from the JAMA paper or PubMed record. One fix: the opening line says 'people who stayed on kept losing' with no 'on average', which turns a group mean into a promise for everyone. Keep the chapter-3 mechanism content attributed to mechanism and label sources, not to SURMOUNT-4. For 'long-term condition', cite a body that actually says it (e.g. WHO's obesity fact sheet calling it a chronic complex disease, or the Obesity Medicine Association). Protein and strength training are 'recommended', with the kidney caveat. No taper or dose numbers. The publisher links How Long.

pieces.topic: Will tirzepatide weaken your bones? Medscape (2 Nov 2026): GLP-1 therapies not linked to fracture risk in three studies, while one real-world cohort linked tirzepatide to higher osteoporosis or fragility-fracture risk than other GLP-1 medicines (HR 1.44)
pieces.angle: Title: 'Tirzepatide and Your Bones: What Studies Show'. Opening: 'Worried tirzepatide could weaken your bones? The evidence so far is mixed, and it all comes from observational studies.' Then: 'Three studies presented at a bone research meeting in 2026, not yet peer-reviewed, didn't link GLP-1 medicines to more fractures.' Then: 'A 2025 database study of adults with type 2 diabetes or obesity linked tirzepatide to a 44% higher rate of new osteoporosis diagnoses or fragility fractures than other GLP-1 medicines. Linked to, not proven to cause.' Then: weight loss by any method can lower bone density; strength training started gently, and protein with a kidney caveat, are recommended. If you have osteoporosis or a history of fractures, ask your doctor about bone health. Add one GI line, 'Don't stop or change your medicines on your own.', the Exp F line, 'Not personal advice' and the prescriber line. Calm visuals; no broken-bone imagery.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide and Bone Loss: Should You Worry?
pieces.why: Fresh hook (Medscape, 2 Nov) on a fear people search for. Our bones Short is our second-best body-worry Short (242 views), and the tirzepatide signal is a new fact. | fact-check: Sources exist. The Medscape piece (2 Nov 2026), 'GLP-1 Therapies Not Linked to Increased Fracture Risk in Three Studies', covers three ASBMR 2026 conference presentations, so those are meeting abstracts that aren't yet peer-reviewed. The HR 1.44 is from Hsu et al., Diabetes Research and Clinical Practice, published online 9 Nov 2025 (PMID 41218687). That study is a retrospective TriNetX cohort of adults with type 2 diabetes OR obesity, with 66,329 per matched group and 14 months of follow-up. Its outcome is a composite of new osteoporosis diagnosis or fragility fracture. Against non-users, HR 1.48 for tirzepatide vs 1.07 for other GLP-1 medicines. It's about a year old, so don't call it 'new'. Problems with the planned opening: (1) 'Most studies so far haven't linked…' overstates things, since the evidence is mixed. A Feb 2026 study (Medscape) found an 11% higher fragility-fracture risk with GLP-1 RAs in older adults with type 2 diabetes. (2) The HR study's outcome is mostly osteoporosis diagnoses, not only fractures, so 'flagged tirzepatide for fractures' is too narrow and too scary. (3) The population includes type 2 diabetes. All of it is observational: 'linked to', never 'causes'. Use absolute incidence only if it's taken from the full paper; if the scriptwriter can't confirm it, say 'the absolute risk was low in both groups' only if the paper says so, otherwise leave absolute numbers out. Watch the overlap with the live Bones & Muscle long-form and last week's bones Short: the new fact here is the ASBMR 2026 findings.

pieces.topic: Retatrutide: what's confirmed vs the 'research peptide' products. A Cureus case report (3 Nov 2026) of liver injury after an unregulated injectable sold as retatrutide, and the Victoria health alert (6 liver-toxicity cases, June 2026)
pieces.angle: Title: 'Retatrutide: What's Actually Confirmed? (Nov 2026)' (keep it, and give the status date as 3 Nov 2026). Beats: (1) retatrutide is still investigational and isn't approved anywhere as of 3 November 2026. Lilly has said it plans to file with the FDA in early 2027, and a plan to file isn't approval. (2) The trial results come from Lilly's drug, given in supervised trials. (3) Online 'research' products aren't the trial drug. In June 2026, Victoria's health department linked six cases of acute liver toxicity to unapproved products labelled retatrutide, possibly from a contaminant, and Australian news later reported a seventh case. (4) If you've used one and notice yellow skin or eyes, dark urine or belly pain, seek medical help right away (Victoria alert wording). Only include a case report you've verified. Then ask a prescriber about approved options or clinical trials, the Exp F line, 'Not personal advice', the prescriber line, and loop back to 'So what's actually confirmed?'
pieces.why: A new case report from today plus seizure news. 'What's confirmed?' retatrutide Shorts with loop endings reached 207–274 views, and this fits the playbook's 13:00 lead options. | fact-check: Verified: the Victoria Department of Health alert (19 June 2026) reports 6 cases of acute liver toxicity since January 2026 linked to unapproved peptide products labelled Retatrutide (also sold as 'Reta', 'R-10', 'R-20'). It says the toxicity is 'possibly associated with a contaminant'. ABC News (24 Aug 2026) reported a seventh Victorian case, so 'six' must be tied to the June alert. Lilly plans to submit to the FDA in Q1 2027 (BioSpace, AJMC). Not approved anywhere is consistent with what I found. NOT verified: a Cureus case report dated 3 Nov 2026. The only Cureus retatrutide case I found was published 26 Aug 2026 and describes GI illness diagnosis challenges after online-sourced retatrutide, not clearly liver injury. Drop the Cureus beat unless the scriptwriter fetches the actual record and confirms its date, title and that it describes liver injury. Don't attribute to Victoria anything it didn't say: it doesn't say the injury was caused by retatrutide itself, and the cause is still under investigation. This counts as the week's single gray-market Short. No sellers, vials, doses, product codes on screen, or sourcing tips.

pieces.topic: Does tirzepatide keep working after month 9? The continued-tirzepatide arm of SURMOUNT-4 (weeks 36–88)
pieces.angle: Title: 'Tirzepatide After 8 Months: Does It Keep Working?' or 'Does Tirzepatide Stop Working Over Time?'. Opening: 'Wondering if tirzepatide stops working after the first eight months? In the SURMOUNT-4 trial, people who stayed on it kept losing a little more weight on average from week 36 to week 88.' Then: '335 people stayed on tirzepatide and lost a further 5.5% of body weight on average. The group switched to placebo regained 14.0% on average. Adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes. Averages, not predictions. Weight loss slowed over time, and plateaus are normal, so talk to your prescriber.' Add one GI line, 'Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own.', 'Not personal advice', the prescriber line, and 'Full breakdown on our channel, link in the description.'
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide After 9 Months: Does It Keep Working?
pieces.why: Spin-off of L1. Funnel Short that corrects a common myth with a new fact (the continued-tirzepatide arm), linking to today's long-form and the Plateau video next to it. | fact-check: A fresh, useful funnel question and a good fit with L1. It's the week's only SURMOUNT-4 Short, which is allowed. Fix the time framing: randomization was at week 36, which is about 8 months, not 9. 'After month 9' / 'After 9 Months' is inaccurate. The continued arm (n=335) lost a further 5.5% of body weight on average from week 36 to week 88 (Aronne et al., JAMA 2024). Copy the exact figure and wording from the JAMA/PubMed record and match L1. Don't say it 'keeps working' for everyone: it's a group average, and the slope flattened over time. Population: adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes. The playbook prefers no number in long titles; one number is allowed in Shorts.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide injection site reactions: what's normal and when to call, reused from the verified 11-02 Short
pieces.angle:
Minimum-effort carousel built only from the verified, published 11-02 S1 script, with no new research. Drop it if that script isn't confirmed as verified.

**Slides:**
1. The question.
2. The label's injection-site reaction rates per dose arm vs placebo, with the terms the label includes, exactly as verified.
3. The verified new fact (the hypersensitivity figures or Taj et al. 2026), exactly as worded.
4. Site rotation, credited to the Instructions for Use only.
5. Call your prescriber for spreading redness, warmth or pus. Get emergency care for swelling of the face, lips or throat, or trouble breathing (label wording).
6. 'Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own.'
7. 'Not personal advice' plus the full prescriber line.

No emoji.
